items.prompt: An unsorted list of scalar measurements must answer whether any two distinct input occurrences differ by at most D. Which sort-based follow-up is sufficient?
constraints: Only existence is required, and original positions are not part of the output.

options.text: Sort ascending and test every adjacent difference.
Sort ascending and compare only the smallest value with every other value.
Sort ascending and compare positions 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, and so on.
Do not sort; test only pairs that were adjacent in the input.

feedback.reason: If any sorted pair is within D, some adjacent pair inside that interval is also within D.

blocks.text: Let x < y be a qualifying non-adjacent sorted pair. Every value between them partitions y - x into adjacent nonnegative gaps, so at least one of those gaps cannot exceed the whole distance and therefore is also at most D. Testing all adjacent gaps is complete. Comparing only selected neighbours or preserving arbitrary input adjacency can miss the local gap that witnesses existence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_first_against_all: A qualifying close pair can occur among larger values even when the smallest value is far from every other value.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_every_other_pair: Skipping alternating adjacent boundaries can omit the only pair whose difference is at most D.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.scan_original_neighbors: Input adjacency is unrelated to numerical distance when the input is unsorted.

items.prompt: Order the operations for a correct minimum-gap scan after receiving an unsorted array with at least two values.
constraints: The output is the minimum absolute value difference.
Original order and indices are irrelevant.

elements.text: Return best after every adjacent boundary has been considered.
Visit each remaining adjacent pair and update best when its gap is smaller.
Initialize best from the difference between sorted positions 0 and 1.
Sort the values in ascending order.

feedback.reason: The scan state is meaningful only after ordering, and the result is final only after every adjacent boundary is covered.

blocks.text: Sorting establishes the invariant that only neighbouring values need comparison. The remaining operations depend on that order and on the stated n ≥ 2 boundary.

items: Sort all values in ascending order so every globally minimum scalar gap has an adjacent witness.
Initialize best from sorted[1] - sorted[0], a real pair guaranteed by n ≥ 2.
For i from 2 through n - 1, compare sorted[i] - sorted[i - 1] with best and retain the smaller gap.
Return best only after every adjacent boundary has been considered.

blocks.title: A prefix optimum is not yet global
blocks.text: Returning before the scan completes can miss a later smaller gap; scanning before sorting compares arbitrary input neighbours and loses the adjacency proof.

items.prompt: After sorting [9, 4, 9, 15], a minimum-gap scan encounters adjacent values 9 and 9. What conclusion is valid?
constraints: The pair may use distinct positions with equal values.

options.text: Remove one 9 and restart the algorithm before recording a result.
The global minimum gap is 0, so the scan may return immediately.
Equal adjacent values must be skipped because they are duplicates.
Continue because a later pair could have a negative gap.

feedback.reason: Zero is the smallest possible absolute difference, and the equal values belong to distinct input positions.

blocks.text: The sorted scan has found a valid pair and reached the lower bound of the objective. No later adjacent difference can improve on zero, so early termination is correct. Deduplicating would erase a material occurrence and could change the answer. This boundary differs from problems that explicitly require distinct values rather than distinct positions; that stronger contract would need to be stated.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.skip_equal_values: Duplicates are precisely the evidence for a zero gap when distinct occurrences are allowed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.continue_for_negative: Absolute differences cannot be negative, so zero is already optimal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.deduplicate_then_restart: Removing an occurrence changes the input multiplicity and discards the valid optimal pair.

items.prompt: Records are sorted by score and then scanned from left to right to return the first adjacent equal-score pair. The contract says that among all such pairs, the lexicographically smallest pair of record IDs must be returned. Which change makes the scan deterministic and contract-complete?
constraints: Several records may share the same score.

options.text: Sort by score only and return the first equal pair produced by the implementation.
Sort by score only, reverse every equal-score run, and return its first pair.
Sort by (score, recordId), take the first two IDs from every equal-score run, and return the lexicographically smallest candidate pair across all runs.
Keep the score-only order but return the final equal pair instead.

feedback.reason: ID tie-breaking exposes the smallest pair inside each score run, but the scan must still compare those run candidates to satisfy a global lexicographic contract.

blocks.text: Sorting by (score, recordId) makes every equal-score class contiguous and orders its IDs ascending. Therefore the first two records in a run form that run's lexicographically smallest valid pair; later members cannot improve its first ID, or its second ID when the first is fixed. Different score runs can have unrelated ID ranges, so the earliest run in score order is not necessarily the global lexicographic winner. The scan must keep the smallest candidate pair seen across all runs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_score_only: The result can vary among legal score-only orders, and returning the first run also confuses score order with the required global ID order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse_each_run: Reversal deterministically chooses large IDs first, the opposite of the requested lexicographic minimum.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.return_last_pair: Changing scan position does not define ID order within a run or compare the best candidates across runs.

items.prompt: A minimum-gap scan must return the original indices of the chosen pair, with smaller original index first. Which representation should the sorted scan consume?
constraints: The output requires two original indices, not positions in the sorted array.

options.text: Only sorted values; use their sorted positions as the answer.
Only original indices sorted numerically, without values.
Only a frequency table, without occurrence identities.
Records (value, originalIndex), sorted by value and then originalIndex.

feedback.reason: The scan needs value adjacency for correctness and original occurrence identity for the required output.

blocks.text: Decorated records preserve both axes. The primary value key establishes the nearest-neighbour theorem, while the index field lets the selected adjacent occurrences map back to the source. An index tie-break makes duplicate-value ordering deterministic but does not replace the final normalization of the returned pair. Raw sorted positions and aggregate frequencies cannot identify which source occurrences were chosen.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_only: Sorted positions describe the transformed array and lose the original-index contract, especially for duplicates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.index_only: Original-index order reveals no value closeness and therefore cannot support the scan proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_frequency: Frequencies can reveal that a zero gap exists but cannot return the two required occurrence indices.

items.prompt: Values are integers from 0 through 1000, and the task is to report which values occur at least twice. Output order is irrelevant. Which assessment is strongest?
constraints: An array of 1001 counters is permitted.

options.text: Use the fixed counter array in O(n + 1001) time; sorting is unnecessary.
Compare every pair because counters cannot represent duplicates.
Sort and binary-search every value to confirm its duplicate count.
Sort first because duplicate detection always needs adjacent equal values.

feedback.reason: The bounded key domain supplies direct grouping state, so sorting adds cost without enabling a missing relation.

blocks.text: A fixed frequency array visits each input once and then inspects a bounded domain. It computes exactly the required predicate while using constant space with respect to n. Sort-then-scan is valid, but not automatically preferable. The choice changes if the domain is huge, memory is constrained, or ascending output is required; those conditions are absent here.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_required: Adjacency is one way to detect duplicates, not a necessary precondition when direct frequency state is available.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pairwise_compare: The counter indexed by value aggregates all occurrences without quadratic comparisons.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_then_binary_search: Binary-searching after a sort repeats work; a single sorted scan would suffice, but the bounded counter is still cheaper here.

items.prompt: An in-place comparison sort with Θ(n log n) worst-case time is followed by a complete adjacent scan with O(1) work per boundary. What is the tightest offered total worst-case time bound?
constraints: No bounded-key non-comparison sorting assumption is available.

feedback.reason: The linear neighbour pass is dominated by the comparison sort's O(n log n) work.

blocks.text: The scan contributes n - 1 constant-time comparisons, so its cost is Θ(n). Adding it to the stated Θ(n log n) sort yields Θ(n log n + n) = Θ(n log n), matching the offered O(n log n) bound. Space depends on the concrete sort implementation and is intentionally not checked.

blocks.title: Why the other offered bounds are wrong
blocks.text: O(n) omits the comparison-sort preprocessing. O(n²) is a valid loose upper bound for ordinary n but is not the tightest offered bound and implies quadratic work that this sort-plus-scan algorithm does not perform.

items.prompt: Select all objectives for which checking every adjacent pair after sorting by a single scalar key is, by itself, a complete candidate search.
constraints: All inputs are finite batch collections.
No additional geometry or graph structure is encoded by the scalar key.

options.text: Minimum absolute difference between any two scalar values.
Closest Euclidean pair of two-dimensional points after sorting only by x-coordinate.
Whether any scalar value occurs at least twice.
Whether any two integers have bitwise XOR equal to a target after sorting numerically.

feedback.reason: Scalar closeness and equality have adjacent witnesses in sorted value order; the other predicates do not.

blocks.text: A globally minimum scalar gap must appear between neighbours, and duplicate values form an adjacent equality boundary. In two dimensions, points close in Euclidean distance can be separated by many points with intermediate x-values, so an adjacent-x-only scan is incomplete. Numeric ordering also gives no monotone rule for XOR equality. The transfer test is the proof of candidate locality, not the visual presence of sorted data.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.closest_2d_points_by_x: Sorting by x is useful in stronger geometric algorithms, but comparing only adjacent x-neighbours does not cover every closest pair.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.pair_xor_target: Bitwise XOR does not vary monotonically with numeric order, so a valid pair can be non-adjacent without an adjacent witness.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.minimum_scalar_gap: One-dimensional order guarantees that any closer non-adjacent pair would contain an at-least-as-close adjacent pair.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_exists: Equal keys occupy one contiguous sorted run, so a duplicate creates an adjacent equal pair.

items.prompt: Why can a sorted array support a linear scan for detecting adjacent duplicate values?

options.text: Equal values become contiguous, so every duplicate pair appears among neighbors.
Sorting deletes all but one copy of each value.
The scan is linear because it performs a binary search for every value.
Sorting preserves the original position of every value automatically.

feedback.reason: Order transforms a global equality question into a local neighbor comparison.

blocks.text: The total cost is O(n log n) for sorting plus O(n) for the scan. No duplicate can be separated by a different value after sorting.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorting_removes_duplicates: Sorting reorders values; it does not remove them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search_each: A direct neighbor scan needs no nested search.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.original_order: Sorting changes positions unless indices are carried as payload.

items.prompt: After sorting distinct integer values, what local comparison reveals whether a gap larger than one exists?

options.text: Check whether sorted[i] - sorted[i-1] > 1.
Check whether sorted[i] + sorted[i-1] > 1.
Compare every value only with the first value.
Check whether the array index is greater than one.

feedback.reason: Sorted adjacency exposes the exact difference between consecutive values.

blocks.text: A difference of one means consecutive integers; a larger difference proves at least one missing integer between the neighbors. The input must be sorted and the arithmetic width must fit the bounds.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sum_gt_one: The sum does not measure the gap between neighboring values.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compare_first: A missing value can occur between two later neighbors even when both relate similarly to the first.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.count_indices: Array positions are not value gaps.

items.prompt: What local fact does sorting provide when scanning for a longest consecutive run?

options.text: Consecutive values can be recognized by comparing adjacent sorted values.
Any pair of values is adjacent after sorting.
The original input order remains available without payloads.
Every run has the same length.

feedback.reason: Sorted adjacency exposes whether the run continues, resets, or skips a gap.

blocks.text: Handle duplicates according to the contract: they may be ignored, reset a strict consecutive run, or count in a frequency-aware variant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random-difference: Only neighboring values are guaranteed to be adjacent.

items.prompt: In a sorted scan for consecutive values, what should happen when the current value exceeds the previous by more than one?

options.text: Reset the current consecutive-run length because a missing value creates a gap.
Extend the run by the full numeric gap.
Delete the values on both sides of the gap.
Move the scan pointer backward until values become adjacent.

blocks.text: The new value can seed a run of length one. The maximum answer retains the best completed run while the current run restarts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.extend-run: Missing integers cannot be counted as present.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.delete-array: Scanning must not mutate input to repair a gap.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.move-back: The sorted scan should continue forward once the boundary is classified.

items.prompt: Why must duplicate handling be stated in a sorted consecutive-sequence scan?

options.text: A duplicate is neither a strict next integer nor necessarily a gap, so the run policy affects the answer.
Every duplicate adds one to a strict consecutive run.
Every duplicate must be removed even when frequency is requested.
Duplicate handling determines the sort comparator only.

feedback.reason: Equal adjacent values need a contract-specific action: skip, reset, or count.

blocks.text: Do not let an accidental <= or < decide duplicate semantics. Write the invariant for the exact sequence definition before coding the scan.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates-always-extend: Strict consecutive values do not advance on equality.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates-always-delete: The requested output may require duplicate frequencies.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicates-sort: Sorting already groups duplicates; policy affects scan state.

items.prompt: What boundary must a run-based sorted scan handle after its loop ends?

options.text: Compare the final current run against the best answer after the last element is processed.
Discard the run because no next value closed it.
Restart from the first element to process the last run.
Always append a real input value to force a boundary.

feedback.reason: The final run may be the longest and has no later differing value to trigger an update.

blocks.text: End-of-input is an explicit scan boundary. Flush or compare the active run before returning the best result.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.discard-final: A valid final run would be lost.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.restart-zero: A second pass is unnecessary when the boundary is handled directly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.add-sentinel-value: A sentinel can be useful only if it cannot collide with input semantics.
